title: Twenty thousand sexes
teaches: Mating types, fused threads and the two-nucleus stage of a mushroom's life
summary: **Most mushroom fungi mate by fusing hyphae.** Two mycelia meet in the soil or wood and join; there are no eggs or sperm.
**Mating types decide who can fuse.** Two mycelia can mate only if their mating-type genes differ.
**After fusing, each cell keeps two nuclei, one from each parent.** The pair divide in step, and the fungus can live this way for years.
**The nuclei fuse only in the gills.** There they join, then divide twice to make four spores, each a new mix of the parents' genes.
**The split-gill mushroom has more than 20,000 mating types.** Two mating-type genes, each with many versions, multiply into that many combinations.
**Many types make almost every stranger a mate.** With many versions, nearly any unrelated mycelium differs, but only a quarter of siblings do, so inbreeding stays rare.
**Many fungi also make spores without mating.** These copies spread a successful fungus fast; sex mixes its genes.

blocks.text: The split-gill mushroom, *Schizophyllum commune*, is one of the most widespread fungi on Earth. It grows on dead branches and logs on every continent but Antarctica, as small, tough, fan-shaped caps a centimetre or two across, grey and furry on top. Turn one over and its gills look as if each had been slit down its edge, which gives it its name. In dry weather the split edges curl over and the cap shrivels; after rain it opens again and goes back to shedding spores.

In the 1950s and 1960s John Raper and his students at Harvard crossed thousands of split-gill strains in the laboratory, pairing them two by two to see which could mate.[^raper] What they found was not two sexes, nor three, but thousands of mating types. Later counts put the total at more than 20,000. Any one of them can mate with almost any other. The question is what so many sexes could be for, and the answer begins with how a fungus mates at all.

Mushroom fungi have no eggs and no sperm. Each spore grows into a mycelium whose cells carry one nucleus each, with a single set of the fungus's genes. When two such mycelia grow into each other in the soil or in a log, their hyphae can meet, open their walls and fuse. That is mating.

What happens next is peculiar to fungi. The two nuclei, one from each partner, do not merge. They pair up and travel together. Every cell of the new mycelium has two nuclei side by side, one from each parent, and when the cell divides they divide in step, so that each new cell again gets one of each.[^clamp] A mycelium of this kind can grow for years, and almost every mushroom you see, and the fairy ring of lesson 1, is built of two-nucleus hyphae. In effect the fungus lives most of its life as a married couple whose genes never mix.

Not every pair can fuse and stay fused. Each mycelium carries **mating-type genes**, and two mycelia can mate only if their versions differ. In many fungi there is a single mating-type gene with just two versions. Baker's yeast is like this: its two types are called *a* and α, and they behave like two sexes, since any *a* can mate with any α and with no other *a*.

The split-gill has two mating-type genes, A and B, and both must differ between partners. In 1920 the German botanist Hans Kniep worked out this two-gene pattern. What Raper's group added was the number of versions of each: hundreds of versions of A and dozens of B. Every combination of an A and a B is a different mating type, which is how the count passes 20,000.

Think of what a mycelium faces. It cannot travel to find a mate. It mates with whoever happens to grow into it, and the most likely partners are its own close relatives, grown from spores of the same mushroom and landing nearby. Mating with a sibling, as in animals, tends to bring out harmful genes and makes offspring less varied.

blocks.caption: The chance that a stranger, or a sibling from the same mushroom, can mate with a given mycelium, as the number of mating-type versions grows. With one gene, partners must differ at it; with two, at both. A model where every version is equally common.
blocks.task: Raise the versions with one gene, then with two

blocks.text: With two versions of one gene, half of all strangers and half of all siblings are possible mates: no help against inbreeding, and half of all meetings wasted. Add versions and a random stranger becomes more and more likely to differ, until almost any unrelated mycelium will do. Siblings, though, only ever carry the two versions their parents had, so the share of compatible siblings stays put. With two genes it falls to a quarter. Many mating types make outbreeding nearly certain and inbreeding rare, without any need to go looking.

Rare versions also have an advantage over common ones: a mycelium with a rare version can mate with almost everyone, so rare versions spread until they are no longer rare. Over long stretches of time this keeps adding versions and keeps them all in use, which is how the split-gill came to have so many.

The two nuclei stay apart through all of the mycelium's growth and through the building of the mushroom. They fuse only at the very end, in the cells on the surface of the gills. There each pair merges into one nucleus with two sets of genes, the only cell in the whole life with both sets together. Almost at once that nucleus divides twice, shuffling and halving the genes, into four new nuclei. Each moves into one of four spores budding on prongs on top of the cell, and those are the spores that Buller's drop throws off.

blocks.caption: The life of a mushroom fungus. Orange and teal mark the two parents' nuclei, purple the one cell where they fuse. Not to scale.

blocks.text: So each spore carries a new combination of its parents' genes, including their mating-type versions. Spores from one mushroom fall in four mating types, and only a quarter of the pairs among them are compatible, which is the sibling figure in the model.

Mating is only half the story. Most fungi can also make spores without it, by pinching off copies from the tips of hyphae. A blue-green mould on an orange, the powdery coat on a leaf, the grey fuzz on a strawberry: these are carpets of copies, made in hours and in vast numbers. A copy has exactly its parent's genes, which is no loss if those genes are doing well on the food at hand.

For some common moulds no one could find a sexual stage at all, and they were classed for a century as fungi that had given sex up. Careful searches keep turning it up. The blue mould used to make Roquefort cheese was shown in 2014 to have both mating types and the genes for mating, and to be capable of sex, after a century of being thought sexless. Copies spread a fungus quickly; sex, now and then, keeps its genes shuffled.

blocks.caption: Five questions on how fungi mate
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How do two mushroom-forming fungi mate?
choices: One releases sperm that swim to the other
Their spores fuse in the air
items.why: Mushroom fungi have no eggs or sperm. Two mycelia grow into each other and their hyphae fuse, if their mating types allow it.

items.ask: What is unusual about a mushroom fungus's cells after mating?
choices: Each has two separate nuclei, one from each parent
Each has no nucleus at all
Each nucleus has four sets of genes
items.why: The partners' nuclei pair up without merging and divide in step. They fuse only in the gills, just before spores are made.

items.ask: How does the split-gill reach more than 20,000 mating types?
choices: Two mating-type genes each come in many versions, and every combination is a type
Every spore makes a brand-new mating type
items.why: Hundreds of versions of one gene times dozens of the other gives tens of thousands of combinations, each a mating type.

items.ask: With many mating-type versions, what happens to the chance that two siblings can mate?
choices: It stays low, because siblings carry only their parents' few versions
It rises to nearly 100%, like strangers
items.why: Siblings share their parents' versions, so many versions in the population do not help them. With two genes, a quarter of sibling pairs can mate, while almost any stranger can.

items.ask: Where do a mushroom fungus's two nuclei finally fuse?
choices: In cells on the surface of the gills, just before spores form
In the spores, after they land
At the moment the two mycelia first meet
items.why: The two-nucleus stage lasts through the mycelium and the mushroom. The nuclei fuse in the gill cells, then divide twice into the nuclei of four spores.

raper.title: Raper's crosses
raper.text: John Raper, a mycologist at Harvard, made the split-gill one of the first fungi whose genetics was worked out in detail. His 1966 book *Genetics of Sexuality in Higher Fungi* laid out the two-gene system, and the fungus is still a standard laboratory species.

clamp.title: Clamp connections
clamp.text: In many mushroom fungi, each time a two-nucleus cell divides, a small hook grows back over the new cross wall and carries one of the dividing nuclei past it. The hooks stay as little bumps beside each cross wall, called clamp connections, and a mycologist looking for them under a microscope can tell at a glance that a hypha has mated.
